q: A customer places an order and the email provider is slow today (5 seconds). With a queue between the API and the email work, about how long does the customer wait, and why?
options: About 5 seconds, because the queue still waits for the email
About 5 seconds, because the queue adds its own delay
Until the worker finishes, which is hidden from the customer
About 60 ms, because the API saves the order, adds a job and answers at once
why: The producer adds a job and moves on. A worker does the slow work later. Without a queue the customer waits the 5 seconds, may see an error, and taps again.

q: A worker takes job 42, sends the email, and crashes before it sends the ack. What happens next?
options: The job is lost, because the worker died
When the hiding timer ends with no ack, the queue shows the job again, and the customer gets a second email
The queue knows the email went out and deletes the job
The worker restarts and the job is skipped
why: The queue cannot see inside the worker. It only knows that no ack came. Most queues show the job again, because a lost job is usually worse than a repeated one. This promise is called at least once.

q: A worker acks the job first, to keep the queue short, and then crashes before it does the work. What is the result?
options: The job is lost and nobody knows, because the queue already deleted it
The job runs twice
The job goes to the dead letter queue
The queue shows the job again after the timer
why: An ack before the work means at most once. Ack after the work, and make the work safe to repeat.

q: A job "add 10 points to a store" can run twice because delivery is at least once. What makes the second run harmless?
options: A longer hiding timer, so the job never runs twice
Telling the queue to deliver exactly once
A unique job id saved in a table with a unique rule, in the same transaction as the points, so the second run finds the id and skips the job
Acking the job first
why: Nobody can promise one single delivery over a network. You build one single effect: at least once delivery plus a worker that is safe to repeat. The check and the work must be one step, or two copies can both pass the check.

q: One job has bad data and fails every time. Someone suggests "retry until it works." What is the better plan?
options: Retry for ever, because the data may fix itself
Delete the job after the first failure
Stop all other jobs until a person fixes it
Retry a few times with growing waits, then move it to the dead letter queue, keep the error and alert a person, while the good jobs keep flowing
why: A job with bad data never works, so retrying for ever wastes the worker and hides the problem. An error that will pass later, like a timeout, gets a retry. An error that never passes goes straight to the dead letter queue.

q: Jobs arrive faster than the workers finish them. No error appears anywhere. What should you watch so you notice?
options: The email provider's error rate only
The queue length and the age of the oldest job
The size of each job
The number of producers
why: A queue grows without noise: the line just gets longer. Alert on the queue length and the age of the oldest job, and on anything in the dead letter queue.
